summary.text: The Wiener process, also called Brownian motion, is a real-valued continuous-time stochastic process named after Norbert Wiener.
A time step u gives an increment that is normally distributed with mean 0 and variance u, its paths are almost surely continuous, and increments over separate periods are independent.
It appears in pure and applied mathematics, economics, quantitative finance, evolutionary biology and physics, and it gave rise to the study of continuous time martingales.

facts.value: A time step u gives an increment with mean 0, variance u

facts.value: Scaling limit of a random walk (Donsker's theorem)

facts.value: Unbounded variation, so not absolutely continuous

facts.value: Recurrent in one or two dimensions, not in three or more

paragraphs.heading: What it is
paragraphs.text: The Wiener process is a random process that runs in continuous time and takes real-number values. It is named after Norbert Wiener, and it is also called Brownian motion because of its historical link with the physical process of that name. It belongs to the Lévy processes, a family whose increments are stationary and independent, and it is one of the best known members of that family.

paragraphs.heading: Its basic properties
paragraphs.text: Write Wₜ for the value of the process at time t. Over a time step of length u, the change, or increment, is normally distributed with mean 0 and variance u, written W_(t+u) − Wₜ ∼ N (0, u). Changes over time periods that do not overlap are independent random variables, and each future change is independent of everything the process did up to now. Its path is also almost surely continuous in time.

paragraphs.heading: Simple numbers
paragraphs.text: These rules lead to simple formulas. The variance of Wₜ is t, so the longer the process runs, the larger its variance. For two times s ≤ t, the covariance of Wₛ and Wₜ is s. Working this out uses only one consequence of the independence of non-overlapping changes: that they are uncorrelated.

paragraphs.heading: The limit of a random walk
paragraphs.text: One way to build the Wiener process is as the scaling limit of a random walk, or of other step-by-step random processes with stationary independent increments; this is Donsker's theorem. For a large number of steps n, the change in the scaled walk between times s and t is, by the central limit theorem, close to N (0, t − s). As n grows without end, the walk approaches a Wiener process. This gives a mathematical explanation for why Brownian motion turns up so often in nature. Like a random walk, the process keeps returning to any neighbourhood of its starting point in one or two dimensions, but not in three or more.

paragraphs.heading: In pure mathematics
paragraphs.text: Within pure mathematics, the study of continuous-time martingales grew out of the Wiener process. It serves as a basic process in terms of which more complicated random processes can be described. That makes it vital to stochastic calculus and to diffusion processes, and it matters even in potential theory. It is also the driving process of Schramm–Loewner evolution.

paragraphs.heading: Across the sciences
paragraphs.text: The process has applications throughout the mathematical sciences. In applied mathematics it represents the integral of Gaussian white noise, so it models noise in electronics, errors of instruments in filtering theory and disturbances in control. Physicists use it to model Brownian motion and other diffusion, often through the Fokker–Planck and Langevin equations, and the Feynman–Kac formula links it to solutions of the Schrödinger equation. It also appears in cosmological models of eternal inflation, and it is prominent in finance, in particular in the Black–Scholes option pricing model.
